1: A condition about an object's state that must hold after every public method returns.
Keeping state private, so that it can change only through methods that protect the rules.
A combination of field values that should never exist, such as a booking with no vehicle.
Reject bad input at once, usually in the constructor or method, instead of carrying it forward.
2: An immutable object compared by its values rather than by identity, such as Money.
A copy made when taking in or handing out a mutable object, so outsiders cannot change internal state.
A small class such as SpotId, so the compiler rejects a VehicleId passed in its place.
Binary floating point cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly, so amounts drift. Use exact units such as paise.
3: What the caller must guarantee before calling a method.
What the method guarantees on return, if the precondition held.
A subtype must be usable wherever its parent type is expected, without surprising the caller.
If a precondition breaks, the caller is at fault. If a postcondition breaks, the method is.
4: One shared test suite that every implementation of an interface must pass.
A deliberately broken implementation, used to prove that the test suite can catch faults.
Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use, so split fat interfaces.
A small interface describing one job that a client needs done.
5: High-level policy and low-level details should both depend on abstractions.
An interface owned by the core of the system, through which it talks to the outside.
The one place where concrete objects are created and wired together.
Single responsibility, Open-closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation and Dependency inversion.
6: One class that knows and does too much, so that every change touches it.
Put interchangeable algorithms behind a shared interface, so that they can be swapped.
A model that allows only named states and legal transitions between them.
You aren't gonna need it: don't build for a need that doesn't exist yet.
7: A return type that names success and each failure, so that the caller must deal with them.
A type that lists its permitted subtypes, so the compiler can check that all cases are handled.
Repeating the same request has the same effect as making it once.
A unique request ID that lets the server recognise a repeat and return the first result.
8: Try again after growing delays, within a limit, so that you don't overload a struggling service.
After repeated failures, stop calling a service for a while and fail fast.
A series of local steps, in which a failure is undone by compensating actions.
Save an outgoing message in the same transaction as the data, then send it separately.
9: The result depends on the timing of threads, as in two threads both taking the last spot.
A read followed by a write based on it. Not safe unless both happen atomically.
Only one thread ever touches the data, so it needs no lock.
Mutable data that is only touched while holding a particular lock.
10: The Java memory model's rule for when one thread's write is guaranteed visible to another's read.
A cluster of objects treated as one unit for changes, which marks a transaction boundary.
Don't lock while reading, then detect a conflicting change at write time, often with a version number.
A database rule that keeps a condition true across transactions and JVMs, which in-memory locks cannot do.
11: One deployable application with strict internal module boundaries.
A translating layer that keeps an outside system's model from leaking into yours.
An automated test that fails the build when a dependency rule is broken.
Arithmetic that estimates load and required resources before any design is drawn.
12: Architecture decision record: a short note of one decision, its context, the options and the consequences.
High-level design: the system's main parts, how they interact, and why.
Tests, measurements and commits that back up each claim made in a design.
What a design gives up to gain something else. A defence must state both sides.
